newsitem.title: UK: Libel case may embarrass Britain's Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Libel case may embarrass Britain's Conservatives.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major may have to give evidence in an explosive libel case starting in London's High Court this week, just before Britain's ruling Conservatives hold a crucial pre-election party conference.
The timing of former trade minister Neil Hamilton's action against the Guardian newspaper over claims he accepted money in exchange for asking parliamentary questions could not be worse.

Major had hoped to use the week-long Conservative conference beginning on October 8 to repair party rifts over Europe and put to rest lingering allegations of sleaze that have dogged his party since he won a five-year term in 1992.

Instead, less than eight months before the next election, he has been subpoenaed to give evidence, along with Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine, in the case which may turn into one of the most sensational political court cases in decades.
Major could become the first British Prime minister to give evidence in court. His lawyers have indicated he would be happy to testify in the case, which is expected to open on Thursday.
"The prime minister and deputy prime minister are concerned to assist and cooperate with this court in arriving at a resolution of the issues to be contested," a statement said.

Hamilton and lobbyist Ian Greer, who works for some of Britain's biggest businesses, are suing the left-leaning Guardian for a reported one million pounds ($1.5 million) over its "cash-for-questions" report in 1994.
The Guardian story accused Hamilton of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the owner of London's luxury Harrods department store, in return for asking questions in parliament.
Hamilton, who resigned as a junior minister over the allegation, has vowed to clear his name, claiming he was a victim of a "foully-motivated rumour and a media witchhunt."
Conservative Party strategists are furious that the trial, which is expected to last four weeks, will begin during the conference season when election campaigns get into full swing.

With the Conservatives trailing the Labour Party by 20 points in opinion polls, and splits over its policy on a single European currency dominating headlines, the party can ill afford any resurfacing of the sleaze factor in politics.

Nearly 20 leading Conservatives have been forced from office over various allegations of impropriety since Major became prime minister in November 1990. This led him to appoint a commission to recommend ways of raising standards in British public life.
